title: Atal's 332-Ball Century Helps Afghanistan Hold Bangladesh to Abu Dhabi Draw
excerpt: Sediqullah Atal made 111 and Qais Ahmad finished unbeaten on 49 as Afghanistan batted 142 overs to finish on 346 for 8, chasing 479.
body:
• Afghanistan batted 142 overs in the fourth innings to finish on 346 for 8, chasing a nominal 479, and draw the one-off Test against Bangladesh in Abu Dhabi.
  • Sediqullah Atal made 111 off 332 balls — the first fourth-innings Test century by an Afghanistan batter — before Qais Ahmad's unbeaten 49 saw out the final session.
  • Bangladesh made 346 and 372 for 7 declared, with Litton Das scoring 53 and 102, but missed a stumping, dropped catches and two run-out chances on the final day.
  • Captain Rahmat Shah, who made 105 in the first innings and 51 in the second, called the result equal to a win for Afghanistan.

Afghanistan held on for a draw that felt like a victory in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, batting through the final day to deny Bangladesh in the one-off Test at the Sheikh Zayed Stadium. Set 479 to win, Afghanistan finished on 346 for 8 after 142 overs in the fourth innings, with two wickets still standing when Qais Ahmad hit the last ball for six.

Bangladesh resumed the final day needing seven wickets, with Afghanistan on 132 for 3. They took wickets at intervals all day — Ebadot Hossain finished with 3 for 50 and Mehidy Hasan Miraz with 3 for 73 — but never the last two. The match, played from October 9 to 13 in severe heat, ended with Bangladesh's fielders still in the field after a full day of bowling.

"This draw is equal to a win, actually."

— Rahmat Shah, Afghanistan captain

Atal's marathon innings

The resistance was built around Sediqullah Atal. The opener, playing only his third Test, scored 111 off 332 balls in eight hours and 34 minutes, with nine fours and three sixes. It was his maiden Test century, the first by an Afghanistan batter in a fourth innings, and, according to ESPNcricinfo, the seventh-longest recorded innings in a fourth innings in Test history.

Atal reached his fifty off 166 balls and survived a missed stumping by Litton Das when he was on 70. He added support from Rahmat Shah, who made 51 off 124 balls, Hashmatullah Shahidi, who made 36 after earlier retiring hurt when struck on the knee, and Ikram Alikhil, who made 33. Atal was finally dismissed eleven overs into the final session, caught at short leg off Taijul Islam, leaving Afghanistan 281 for 7 with about 23 overs left.

That should have opened the door. Instead, Qais Ahmad, batting at No. 9, made an unbeaten 49 off 80 balls, and Yamin Ahmadzai faced 85 balls for 19. Their eighth-wicket stand lasted more than 18 overs. When Ahmadzai fell to Miraz, Qais and Zia-ur-Rehman saw out the remaining overs.

Missed chances cost Bangladesh

Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto pointed to the fielding. Qais was dropped at silly point and later at deep mid-wicket. Bangladesh missed two run-out opportunities off consecutive deliveries. Ahmadzai edged the ball onto his stumps without dislodging the bails. On a pitch that offered bowlers little, those moments were the match.

"We should have taken all ten wickets today."

— Najmul Hossain Shanto, Bangladesh captain

Shanto credited his bowlers for working through 142 overs in the conditions and said Bangladesh had played good cricket across five days, but accepted that small mistakes decided the result. He also praised Litton Das, who was named player of the match after scores of 53 and 102 and a heavy workload behind the stumps in the heat.

How Bangladesh built their position

Bangladesh won the toss and made 346 in the first innings, led by Tanzid Hasan's 83, Shadman Islam's 67 and Litton's 53, against Mohammad Saleem's 4 for 82. Afghanistan replied with 240, despite Rahmat Shah's 105 and Abdul Malik's 62, as Hasan Mahmud took 5 for 55.

With a lead of 106, Bangladesh declared their second innings at 372 for 7. Litton made 102, Shanto 82 and Mushfiqur Rahim 81, setting a target that was meant to be about time, not runs. Afghanistan understood that clearly. Rahmat said his side had planned for both situations — scoring when runs were available and occupying the crease when survival was the task — and had followed that plan.

What it means

For Afghanistan, a side still building its Test record, surviving 142 overs in a fourth innings against a more experienced attack is a substantial result, whatever the scorebook calls it. For Bangladesh, the lesson is narrower and harder: on a flat pitch in Abu Dhabi, creating chances was not enough. They needed to take all of them, and on the final day they did not.

For diaspora fans, the draw was a reminder of what Test cricket does best — a result with no winner, decided by patience and one opener who refused to leave.
